fine_trace.note: Attacker-controlled Ruby program executes OP_ARYCAT (array literal with splat `[*foo]`). The operand regs[a+1] is a user object whose class defines a `to_a` method, so mrb_ary_splat will dispatch a nested Ruby call.

The guard confirms the dangerous precondition: the splat operand responds to to_a AND the callinfo stack c->cibase is exactly full (ci is the last slot), so the next cipush (from the nested to_a call) will realloc/free the cibase buffer that the outer frame's cached `ci` still points into.

fine_trace.code: mrb_value ary = mrb_funcall_argv(mrb, v, MRB_SYM(to_a), 0, NULL);
fine_trace.note: mrb_ary_splat invokes the attacker-defined to_a method on the operand, entering a nested mrb_vm_exec while the outer mrb_vm_exec still holds a cached ci pointer into the old cibase.

Root cause: the nested to_a call pushes a callinfo via cipush; because the cibase was exactly full, mrb_realloc frees the old callinfo buffer and allocates a new one. The outer mrb_vm_exec frame's cached `ci` still points into the freed old buffer. Safety condition that should hold: the outer ci must remain within the live cibase (ci < c->ciend), i.e. ci must be re-derived after any nested call that can grow cibase.

Sink: after mrb_ary_splat returns, the outer VM continues executing OP_ARYCAT using `regs` (macro for ci->stack) with the stale ci that points into the freed cibase; dereferencing regs[a] reads freed heap memory (heap-use-after-free in mrb_vm_exec). The instrumented build confirms this by printing ASSERT_EVT point=arycat_sink at this opcode when a cipush_realloc occurred during the splat.
